questions.question: What does Node 24 do when you run `node app.ts`?
options: Type-checks the file and refuses to run it if there are type errors
Strips the type annotations and runs the result without type-checking
Compiles enums and parameter properties into JavaScript, then runs it
Requires a tsconfig.json before it will run any .ts file
questions.explanation: Node's built-in support only strips erasable type syntax. It never type-checks, and it rejects syntax that needs code generation, such as enums and parameter properties. Keep tsc --noEmit in CI for actual checking.

questions.question: In Express's `Request<A, B, C, D>`, which type argument describes the request body?
questions.explanation: The order is route params, response body, request body, query string. So the third argument (C) types req.body.

questions.question: A handler is typed `Request<{}, unknown, CreateFundBody>`. A client posts `{ "navInr": "lots" }`. What happens?
options: Nothing stops it: the type is only a compile-time claim, so the bad data reaches your code unless you validate it
TypeScript rejects the request with a 400 response
Express converts navInr to a number automatically
questions.explanation: Types are erased at runtime. Annotating req.body does not check incoming data, so you must validate at the boundary, for example with a schema library.

questions.question: Why is `process.env.DATABASE_URL` typed as `string | undefined`?
options: Because environment variables can only be strings in Windows
Because any environment variable may be missing at runtime, so the type honestly includes undefined
Because strict mode adds undefined to every property
questions.explanation: Nothing guarantees a variable is set. The recommended pattern is to read and validate env vars once at startup, throwing if a required one is missing, and export a typed config object.
